title: The colour that fell to earth
text: Prussian blue, the first great synthetic pigment, began as a laboratory {{1}}. Around 1706, a Berlin colour-maker tried to make a red from cochineal, borrowing potash that had been {{2}} with animal blood; the mixture turned a deep, brilliant blue, and within a few years the pigment was in {{3}} across Europe. Painters seized on it: deeper and far cheaper than ultramarine, which was still ground by hand from lapis lazuli {{4}} from Afghan mines, it spread through eighteenth-century art at {{5}} speed — Hokusai's Great Wave is printed in it, as are the skies of Watteau and Gainsborough. Chemistry later {{6}} the accident: the iron in the blood and the potash had formed a compound of unusually intense colour. The same compound turned out to {{7}} certain heavy metals in the digestive tract, and it is still used in poisoning treatment today. No one planned any of it. Prussian blue is what happens when the {{8}} gets lucky — a reminder that science advances sideways as often as forwards.

gaps.explanation: 'began as a laboratory accident' — an unplanned event; incident = a distinct (often unpleasant) event.
'potash contaminated with animal blood' — accidentally made impure; concoct = invent or mix up.
'the pigment was in circulation' — moving from user to user; calibration = fine adjustment of instruments.
'lapis lazuli hauled from Afghan mines' — dragged over great distance; hamper, halt and house do not describe getting stone to Europe.
'at remarkable speed' — strikingly fast; stagnant = not moving at all.
'chemistry later illuminated the accident' — explained it, keeping the light metaphor; eliminate = remove.
'turned out to bind certain heavy metals' — attach them firmly so they cannot be absorbed; bound is the past participle.
'when the laboratory gets lucky' — the workplace of the accident; laudatory = full of praise.
